positive: Many commenters are eager and counting down to pre-order, with some planning to order the moment sales open regardless of price.
Several name the configuration they intend to buy, most often white with large storage such as 512GB or more, sometimes unlocked.
Some admit they don't really need it but are being won over by the design, video-viewing and reading appeal, or a review.
Many commenters say they are excited and plan to buy or preorder the Duo as soon as it is released.
Viewers like the clean design and the large foldable screen, and some had wanted a foldable iPhone without leaving iOS.
Some accept missing features or weaker cameras for a new type of Apple device, though a few would wait for a later generation.
negative: Many commenters say the price is far too high, joking that buying the phone would cost them a lot of money, or even a kidney.
Some plan to hold off, either waiting for a later version or to see whether the foldable screen creases or breaks.
Others mock Apple's naming and marketing, and criticise buyers who say they don't care about the features but purchase it anyway.

positive: Many commenters say they plan to buy the phone anyway, shrugging off warnings and criticism from reviewers.
Some accept the drawbacks, such as Touch ID and no telephoto lens, because they like the design and interface.
A few plan to soften the high price with interest-free financing or retailer perks like free AppleCare.
negative: Price is the main objection: commenters see the foldable as far too expensive, especially at higher storage tiers once tax is included, and some urge a boycott.
Apple is seen as copying existing foldables, and some say Android phones are the better choice for camera quality.
Features such as built-in MagSafe are called pointless because most people use a case, and some extras are seen as wasteful.

positive: Several commenters defend or accept the high cost, arguing the foldable design and the software are novel enough to justify paying more.
Some say the price makes sense because the device works like two phones in one, valuing multitasking and larger-screen reading or viewing.
Others say they would skip the top camera and pay for the form factor and a smaller folded size, though some admit they cannot afford it.
negative: Many commenters see the roughly $2,000 starting price as excessive for a phone and say they would not pay it.
Some feel the price is poor value, citing modest storage on the base model, only two cameras, and a missing dust and water rating.
Others worry about costly repairs and durability, since the fold may wear out and a protective case makes the phone bulky.

positive: Many commenters on older Pro models plan to trade in and upgrade to the Duo, saying it feels like a fresh, more exciting change.
Several say they rarely use pro-level cameras, so giving those up for the Duo's larger screen and tablet-like use seems an easy choice.
Some see the Duo as lightening their load by replacing a tablet or laptop, while a few keep a Pro Max for photos.
negative: Many commenters say the Duo's price is too high, especially when a Pro Max or their current phone already meets their needs.
Camera downgrades versus the Pro line (no main-lens match, less telephoto, fewer lenses) and missing Face ID are frequent deal-breakers.
Several would rather buy the Pro Max, or wait for a later Duo version, citing unknowns, little need for the inner screen and heat worries.

positive: Many commenters who own a Samsung Fold say they are happy with it, while some also admit Apple's first foldable impressed them.
Samsung supporters credit its customisation, innovation and long foldable experience, and say Apple's entry will push Samsung to improve, for example by restoring stylus support and water resistance.
Others argue Apple's strength is ecosystem and refinement, and that its price looks reasonable for a first-generation foldable.
negative: Many commenters say Apple is late to foldables and is copying Samsung, which has sold them for years, and they mock the way Apple presents the idea as new.
Several complain about the high price, including that it costs more than Samsung's newest folds in some regions. They say it should have top cameras and other strengths.

Others compare specs and tradeoffs: the Apple model is heavier, and Samsung's thinner design gives up some features. Some also question its durability rating and Samsung's software, while Face ID gets praise.

positive: Many commenters praise Apple's polish: the fold transition, animations and UI design are seen as thoughtful and distinctly Apple, and some are surprised at how good a first foldable is.
Ecosystem loyalty is strong. Some Apple users waited for an Apple foldable instead of buying Android ones, preferring iOS simplicity and trusting Apple's build quality.
Some note that Apple is often copied or that Android already offers multitasking and flexibility, but they see competition and shared ideas as good for consumers.
negative: Many commenters say Apple copies Android and Samsung features, arrives years late, and has run out of original ideas.
Apple fans are accused of hypocrisy for mocking foldables as gimmicks before and now embracing them once Apple releases one.
Others criticise Apple's pricing, first-generation reliability and hardware quality, though a few raise practical worries like repair access and input lag.

positive: Many praise the matte inner screen, saying it looks attractive, helps hide the crease, and suits long reading sessions.
The transition between the outer and inner screens when folding or unfolding is described as smooth, clean and polished.
Commenters like the larger pocketable display for multitasking and bigger text, and say the screen and minimal crease impress them.
negative: Many see the inner screen as a downgrade: matte anti-reflective finish, less sharpness than the outer display, and a crease that seems merely hidden rather than solved.
Durability and repair costs worry commenters: past foldable screens failed after about a year, and a cracked screen could mean costly repairs or high AppleCare fees.
The outer screen and size draw complaints: it is small for daily use, awkward for left-handed users, and the extra inner space seems not worth the price.

positive: Commenters prefer a hidden under-display camera over a hole punch or notch, valuing an uninterrupted full screen despite criticism from reviewers.
Many say selfies would mostly be taken with the outer display camera, so a slightly weaker inner camera matters little.
The matte inner display is praised for hiding the crease and giving a clean look, seen as a standout feature.
negative: Several commenters say under-display cameras were abandoned because of poor image quality, and some see them as a downgrade.
The inner screen draws complaints: it looks grainy, colors seem inaccurate, and the matte finish loses the glossy OLED look some people want.

positive: Many commenters praise the open and close animation as smooth, clean and seamless, and say the design team deserves credit.
Several like the blur and see-through glass effect, calling it clever and an example of Apple making something simple feel obvious.
Some, including self-described Samsung fans, think the animation could drive sales and say it is a standout feature of the foldable.
negative: Commenters mock the idea that a fold or unfold animation is a headline feature, saying it reflects poorly on the phone's overall merits.
Several say the animation is just a simple blur effect and not impressive enough to be a selling point.
Some point out glitches in the screen animation when closing, and criticise how fans prioritise polish over features.

positive: Many left-handed commenters say they already hold or use phones in their right hand, so the design doesn't bother them.
Lefties describe a lifetime of adapting to right-handed devices and see this as manageable, not a deal breaker.
Some think the concern is overblown and expect a software setting to mirror or rotate the layout for left-handed users.
negative: Left-handed users say the dual-screen design appears built for right-handed use and would be awkward or frustrating for them.
Some worry that unlocking with Face ID would be especially difficult for left-handed people, and say it makes them hesitant to buy.
Several commenters mock the idea of telling left-handed users they are holding it wrong, suggesting the design overlooks them.

positive: Pencil support is a major selling point for several commenters, who see it as a reason to choose or upgrade to the Duo.
Many want to use the larger inner screen for sketching, painting and productivity, treating it like a mini iPad that also works as a phone.
Some Android foldable owners say the lack of pen support on their devices is a drawback, making Apple's compatibility feel like a missed opportunity for them.
Commenters liked the form factor and software, including the side toolbar and button placement, and saw uses in reading, navigation, medical work, and retro-style gaming.
Several said the camera compromises don't bother them, since they mainly use their phone for scrolling and media or rely on a separate camera.
negative: Many see the foldable as essentially a small iPad in phone form, so they question its point and say a regular iPad makes more sense.
The high price is a major complaint; commenters say it costs more than an iPad and isn't justified by the camera setup or niche use.
Skeptics doubt the unfolded screen will be used much, expect early software problems, and worry about the crease and awkward shape, so some would wait for later generations.

positive: Many commenters are excited about the foldable's new, different design, calling it the most interesting iPhone in years and a break from the older look.
Several say they plan to buy it, including long-time Apple users and some Android users who admire it, while a few are waiting for next year's models.
Some praise practical design points: multitasking on a bigger screen, a durable titanium build, slim bezels and a hidden front camera, with hopes for tougher screen glass.
negative: Many commenters say the foldable is very heavy, likely the heaviest iPhone yet, and a case would make one-handed use hard.
Some joke that Apple will advertise small improvements, such as a less visible crease or lighter weight, in later generations.
Others see the design as copying rivals' foldables and question the name, with some preferring a flip style over a book-style fold.

positive: Many commenters are very excited and plan to preorder or buy the Duo, often saying desire comes first and justification later.
Viewers like the book-like opening, the hardware and software fit, and the fold-hiding screen, and see earlier products as stepping stones.
People expect it to suit media, reading and multitasking, and hope features like the hidden selfie camera carry into future iPhones.
negative: Commenters see the Duo as too expensive, with high base prices and storage upgrades, and regional markups and carrier lock-ins make it less appealing.
Many criticise its weight, thickness, and camera compared with Pro models, and expect case, balance, or durability problems.
Some say rival foldables offer more features or better value, and doubt that Apple users want a foldable or that comparisons are fair.

positive: Commenters like the polished software transitions and expect developers, including big names like Netflix, to adapt apps, which could also improve iPad versions.
Many see two apps side by side as a sensible, sufficient level of multitasking, and some like it for reading or other uses.
negative: Commenters doubt the multitasking features are useful, saying they look like hype or marketing aimed at a niche, wealthy audience rather than a real need.
Several say the app-dragging and window-arranging behaviour feels borrowed from tablet software, and portrait multitasking seems limited to small pop-up video windows.
Some dislike the button layout, such as the placement of volume and silent controls, and the loss of the old mute switch.

positive: Several commenters prefer a fingerprint scanner to Face ID, saying it feels faster and more reliable, and that it doesn't need an Apple Watch as a workaround.
Some feel more comfortable with fingerprint unlocking because they see constant face scanning as a privacy concern.
A few viewers praise the phone's polished, high-tech look, and say it makes them more interested in buying one.
negative: Some viewers see the lack of Face ID, paired with a triple camera setup, as a puzzling choice and are waiting for later models.
Several comments say the design feels unambitious or derivative, citing wasted screen space and an interface that doesn't use the form factor well.
High pricing draws criticism, with the sense that Apple charges a lot without matching it with real innovation or key features like Face ID.
